query: More than a century of research on conventional steels and other alloys has shown that exposure within certain temperature ranges can sharply reduce toughness and threaten safety in aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical applications. High-entropy alloys offer attractive strength, ductility, resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement, and wear resistance; however, their multicomponent chemistry complicates predictions of long-term mechanical reliability. Their resistance to rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation does not establish whether their toughness will remain stable after service-relevant heating, and this uncertainty limits engineering use. For a high-performance multicomponent high-entropy alloy in its as-designed condition, under the constraint that its original strength–ductility combination must be retained, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to reduce post-exposure toughness degradation? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to an otherwise identical untreated baseline, define the temperature, duration, and loading boundaries, identify supporting evidence from the observations summarized above, and describe a decisive experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of tungsten carbide (WC) to a high-entropy alloy (HEA) will reduce post-exposure toughness degradation after service-relevant heating.
generation.intervention: Addition of a small amount of tungsten carbide (WC)
generation.conditions: Service-relevant heating, with temperature range between 600°C to 1000°C, and duration of 100 hours
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable solid solution structure with dispersed WC particles
generation.mechanism: The dispersed WC particles will act as obstacles to dislocation movement, reducing the formation of deleterious intermetallic phases and grain coarsening, thus retaining the alloy's toughness
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced post-exposure toughness degradation, with a predicted toughness retention of at least 80% compared to the untreated baseline
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy with the same composition and processing history
generation.boundary: Temperature range between 600°C to 1000°C, duration of 100 hours, and loading conditions of up to 500 MPa
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of WC to be added and the optimal processing conditions to achieve the desired microstructure are uncertain and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative study of the toughness of the WC-added HEA and the untreated baseline after service-relevant heating
measurements: Toughness measurements using Charpy impact testing
Microstructural analysis using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the toughness of the WC-added HEA is not significantly higher than that of the untreated baseline, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys consist of alloying elements with five or more equal molar fractions, each of which has a molar fraction of about 5% to 35%. As a kind of comprehensive material, high entropy alloy has better physical and chemical properties than many common metal compounds []. Therefore, it has attracted wide attention in material science and engineering and is the focus field of scholars at home and abroad [,]. In recent years, many scholars at home and abroad have used high entropy alloys for surface modification, mainly by laser melting, laser deposition, and plasma melting. The lower preparation cost and excellent performance of high entropy alloys not only improve their service life and significantly reduce the failure loss but also reduce their surface repair cost, and high entropy alloys have many advantages that traditional alloys can hardly match []. However, there are difficulties in the synergistic enhancement of strength, toughness, and corrosion resistance of high entropy alloys, and no satisfactory solution has been found so far []. Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,]. The concept of high entropy alloy (HEA) was proposed and published in 2004 [,,] and the unique properties of these alloys have attracted attention from research groups all over the world. The pioneering studies by Cantor et al. were the first to report that an equiatomic alloy consisting of the five transition metals Cr, Mn, Fe, Co and Ni crystallized as a single solid solution [,] in the as-cast and in the homogenized state. The first HEA generation could contain five or more main elements with the concentration of each element in the range 5–35 at. % []. The alloys presented a high mixing entropy in their liquid state [] and thus could form simple solid solution structures (e.g., FCC, BCC and HCP) in place of intermetallic phases. Some promising technological characteristics of HEAs were high hardness [], good wear resistance [], excellent strength at both high and low temperatures [,,] and generally a good resistance to oxidation and corrosion [].
